note.p: Daughter of King Oedipus of Thebes and his mother, Jocasta. In Sophocles's Antigone, she fights for a proper burial for her brother, Polyneices, who was thought to be a traitor to Thebes.
English Elizabethan poet and soldier. Wrote Astrophel and Stella.
Older brother of Moses and a prophet.
Greek god of rebirth and vegetation.
Athenian Tragic Dramatist.
Ancient Greek Sophist and epistlographer.
A Greek demi-goddess, the daughter of Aeolus and wife of Ceyx, son of Eosphorus and the king of Thessaly.
Italian dramatist.
The great god of Egyptian Thebes, sometimes identified with Zeus. And name given to the oracle of the Temple of Ammon in Siwa. The oracle was thought to be the son of Zeus.
Lover of the Greek poet Sappho.
Character appearing in the sixth tale of the forth day in Boccaccio's Decameron. She is forced to proclaim her innocence after her lover, Gabriotto, dies when she recounts to him a recent dream.
Fictional author of the fictional epigraph to Swinburne's Laus Veneris.
Goddess of love and beauty, who rose from the sea born from the severed genitals of Uranus.
Greek god of music and poetry, son of Zeus and Leto.

A character in Shakespeare's and John Fletcher's play, The Two Noble Kinsmen. He battles with Palamon to win the hand of Emilia. Though victorious, he dies when thrown from his horse after the battle and Theseus allows Palamon to marry Emilia.
Daughter of Merops of Percote, a seer, and wife of the future Trojan king, Priam.
Famous writer of old Greek Tragedy in the 5th century B.C.

birth.date: mid 1st century B.C. - early 1st century A.D.

note.p: Wife of A. Ceacina Paetus, who had be ordered to commit suicide for rebellion against Claudius and the Roman Empire. She stabbed herself in order to alleviate her husband's fear of death.
Greek goddess of child birth, virginity, and the hunt. She was thought to be the daughter of Zeus and Leto and the twin sister of Apollo.
Canaanite fertility goddess.
A demon.
Semitic goddess of fertility and love.
Daughter of Cranaus, who named the region of Attica after her early death.
The consort of Cybele whose priests were eunuchs as well as the Phrygian god of vegetation.
Eldest daughter of Zeus, who was condemned to earth when Zeus found out that she was working with Hera to secure prosperity for Hera's son, Eurystheus, over Heracles.

Balin and his brother Balan are two tragic Arthurian figures, brothers who despite their nobility end up killing one another. Their story is recounted in Malory's Morte d'Arthur, Tennyson's Idylls of the King, and Swinburne's The Tale of Balen.
French republican in the mid-nineteenth century who was sentenced to life in prison twice for trying to overthrow the monarchy.
In ancient Greece, a devotee of Bacchus.
English poet and artist.
French politician and historian. Influential in the development of socialism, especially in France.
Italian author, wrote the Decameron. Friend and correspondent of Petrarch.
English writer. Author of A Year in a Lancashire Garden (London: Macmillan, 1879).
English poet famous for his use of dramatic monologue.
Italian philosopher who was burned at the stake in Rome because of the perceived heresy of his philosophy.
A Roman senator, who played a leading role in the assination of Julius Caesar.
English artist and designer during the late Pre-raphelite movement.
English explorer and ethnologist. Best now for his explorations within Asia and Africa. Friend of Swinburne.
A Phonecian who became the founder of the ancient city of Thebes.
Mother of the five Cairoli brothers, Italian patriots, all of whom fought and four of whom died in the struggle for Italian unification.
Greek poet and scholar in the 3rd century B.C.
A Dominician who played a role in bringing the papacy backed to Rome (from Avignon) and establishing peace among the Italian city-states.
Roman poet.
English translator, dramatist, and poet.
Mother of Tiresias, the blind Cadmean prophet. According to the Greek poet, Callimachus, she begged Athena to restore Tiresias's vision, which lead Athena to give him foresight.
English poet, writer, and statesman. Wrote the The Canterbury Tales.

death.date: Around the beginning of the 4th century BC

note.p: Greek epic poet.
English poet and critic. One of the founders of Romanticism. Cowrote Lyrical Ballads.
Greek epic poet.
Greek poet.
Roman Emperor from 306 to 337 who is well known for converting to Christianity and issuing the Edict of Milan in 313 wich proclaimed tolerance of all religions throughout the empire.
17th-century French tragic dramatist.
Famous Roman mother and wife. Wife of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus and mother of the Gracchi, her two sons, both statesmen and social reformers who were killed in political violence.
Thracian goddess of immodesty and debauchery, who is worshipped with orgiastic rites of song and dance.
English soldier and statesman, lord protector of the republican Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1653-58).

The Anatolian Earth Goddess and "Great Mother of the Gods" whose worship was characterized by ecstatic states and insensibility to pain. Her cult was based in Phyrgia and spread to Asia Minor and Greece.
Florentine poet during the Middle Ages. Wrote the Divine Comedy.
The most important Greek oracle and consultant of the growing Greek empire. Also known as the Oracle or priestess of Apollo.
Son of Zeus and Semele and Greek god of wine and ecstasy.
She was the wife of Lycus, who had been killed by Amphion and Zethus for the maltreatment of their mother, Antipone, by tying her to the horns of a bull.
Ancient Greek oracle, possibly the oldest of the oracles. She was located in the northwest part of Greece and typically would advise people on personal issues.
Illustrator. His work appeared frequently in Punch magazine.
A Thracian tribe living about Mount Pangaeüs. Known in myth for the persection of Bacchus and his followers by the Edonian King Lycurgus.
Greek Stoic philosopher and former slave.
Wife of Orpheus. She was killed when bitten by a snake and sent to the Underworld, where Orpheus entered to get her back.
Goddesses of beauty and charm and attendants of Aphrodite.
Born Pierre Roger de Beaufort. Pope from 1370 to 1378. Gregory XI was the last of the Avignon Popes.
Goddess of harmony and concord and daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. She married Cadmus and became Queen of Thebes.
German writer and poet. Lived in Paris after 1831.
Son of Zeus and Alcmene and Greek hero.
Son of Aphrodite and Hermes. He was transformed into an androgynous being due to his encounter with the naiad, Salmacis.
Germanic earth and fertility goddess.
Nymphs who live in a garden in the Arcadian Mountains on the western extreme of the Mediterranean. In the garden, they guard the tree of golden apples given by Gaia to Hera upon her marriage to Zeus.
Amazonian Queen abducted by Theseus. She was Theseus' first wife. In Greek mythology she possessed a magical girdle given to her by her father, Ares, the god of war.
Son of Theseus. He was killed when his startled horses dragged him to his death. In Greek mythology, Theseus employed the gods to kill his son because of his supposed rape of Phaedra.

birth.date: Between the 8th century and 9th century BC

death.date: Between the 8th century and 9th century BC

note.p: Greek epic poet. Attributed having written the Iliad and the Odyssey.
French writer, novelist, playwright, and poet who was idolized by Swinburne. Wrote The Hunchback of Notre Dame.
A prostitute who was occassionally the subject of Catullus' poetry.
In the story of Tristan and Iseult, she is supposed to marry King Mark of Cornwall. But in route to the king, she and Tristan accidentely consume a love potion and fall in love with one another.
Major Egyptian goddess. Embodiment of maternal power and virtue. Mother of Horus, first ruler of a united Egypt.
Son of Aedon. He was accidently killed by Aedon when in envy she tried to kill Niobe's eldest son.

death.date: Between the second and forth decade in the 1st century AD

note.p: Born to Mary and Joseph in Bethlehem. According to most Christian faiths, Jesus, the Son of God, was born of the Virgin Mary, who conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit. Jesus was a religious leader proclaiming the coming of God's kingdom and was crucified by order of the Roman prefect, Pontius Pilate, for high treason.
A military leader who led the French in several victories over the English in the Hundred Years War. She was captured in 1430 and burned at the stake for heresy.
One of the Twelve disciples of Jesus. He betrayed Jesus's location to Jewish authorities for money.
Roman Emperor from 361 to 363 and also a philosopher who purged the top-heavy state bureaucracy and attempted to revive traditional Roman religious practices instead of Christianity
English poet.
Legendary British leader who led the British defense againt the Saxon invaders in the beginning of the 6th century.
A character in Dante Aligheri's Purgatory, thought to be based upon Pia Tolomei, who was killed in 1295 on the orders of her husband.
English/Welsh essayist.
English Romantic poet. Author of Gebir and prose “imaginary conversations.” Republican.
New Testament figure, raised from the dead by Christ (John 11:1-43).

French editor and publisher, known as a publisher of many of the Paranssian poets in his three-volume collection Le Parnasse contemporain (1866, 1871, 1876). Edited Le Tombeau de Théophile Guatier (1871), in which Swinburne's work appears.
An Italian poet, writer, and philosopher.
In Roman mythology, the godess of corpses and funerals.
Roman Emperor from 308 to 324 who coauthored the Edict of Milan and was eventually executed on the orders of Constantine I.
A pseudonymn for Valumnia Cytheris, a freedwoman, actress, and mistress of Mark Antony and Cornelius Gallus, given her by Gallus in his four books of elegies.
English Elizabethan playwright and contemporary of William Shakespeare. His Tamburlaine was one of the first English plays in free verse, the form later made famous by Shakespeare.
French aristocrat, revolutionary politician, philosopher, and writer famous for his libertine sexuality and lifestyle.
One of the inner circle of followers of Jesus. She witnessed the crucifixtion and was one of the first witnesses of Jesus' resurrection.
Mother of Jesus. Known as the Virgin Mary because she was said to have conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Sole surviving legitimate child of King James VI, King of Scotland. She was made queen of Scotland at six days old. She was imprisoned in Loch Leven Castle and later executed by Queen Elizabeth the First for fear she would abdicate the English crown.
Italian patriot, idolized by Swinburne.

The son of Althaea, the queen of Calydon, whose love for Atalanta led to his killing of Althaea's brothers and, in turn, his death when Althaea intentionally placed a brand on the fire that the fates had predicted would bring the end of Meleager' life.
Seventeenth-century English poet. Author of Paradise Lost and Samson Agonistes. Republican and official in Cromwell's Commonwealth.
English painter, poet, and artist. Friend of Swinburne, associated with the Pre-Raphelite movement.
Son of a sheppard, who witnessed the presence of God in a buring bush near Horeb in the Sinai region of Egypt. He was given the Ten Commandments and told to lead the Hebrews out of Egypt.

person.persName: Napoleon I, Emperor of the French

note.p: French general during the later years of the Revolution (1788-1799) and, later, the Consul and renown Emperor of France.
Roman emperor from 54-68 C.E.. Known for being the emperor during the great fire of Rome in 64 C.E..

Wife of Tantalus, the King of ancient Sipylus, who gave birth to 14 children. In Greek mythology her bragging about her fertility upset Leto, who employed her 2 children, Apollo and Artemis to kill Niobe's children.
Thebean king, who, according to Sophocles, unknowingly killed his father and marries his mother.
Son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra. He killed his mother in revenge for her murder of Agamemnon.
He was considered the greatest musician and poet of Greek myth, who used his song most notably to save the Argonauts from the Sirens and to attempt bringing his wife back from the Underworld.
He tried to usurp the Athenian crown from Thesues, but was killed in an ambush near Gargettus.
Daughter of Helios, the sun, and wife of King Minos of Crete. A curse by Posiedon forced her to copulate with a bull and give birth to the Minotaur.

A immortal, winged horse who carried the thunder and lightening of Zeus. It was said that the Pegasus would make a spring every time it stamped its hoof on the ground. Hippocrene on Mt. Helicon was thought to be one of the Pegasean-made springs.
Early Christian ascetic and theologian.

A king of Thebes and son of Agave and Cadmus. According to Euripidies, Pentheus unknowingly imprisons a disguised Dionysus. In retribution, Dionysus has Pentheus torn apart by a group of maenads led by Pentheus's mother.
One of the twelve apostles. Originally named Simon, but given the name Peter by Jesus. Attributed with 1 & 2 Peter.
Second wife of Theseus. She killed herself because her lie about Hippolytus raping her led to his death.
Ancient Greek Lyrical poet.
King of Troezen, a city in northeastern Peloponnese. He alone understood the prophesies of Aegeus, one of the founders legendary Athens.
The seven daughters of the Titan, Atlas, who accompanied Artemis.
Wife of Brutus, who was the leader in assassination of Julius Ceasar.
Welsh squire and poet. Swinburne's roundels A Dead Friend, Past Days, and Autumn and Winter, memorialize Powell without naming him explicitly.
In Greek mythology, a god of fertility.
A Sophist, travelling teacher of higher education, particularly Rhethoric. He was a contemporary of Socrates.
Goddess of the Underworld and daughter or Zeus and Demeter in Greek mythology. Called Persephone by the Greeks and Proserpina or Proserpine by the Romans.
English poet. Sister of Dante Gabriel and William Michael Rossetti. Friend of Swinburne's.

Victorian English writer, artist, art critic and theorist, and social commentator. Famous works include Modern Painters, The Stones of Venice,, and his autobiography Praeterita. Ruskin was a passionate supporter of J.M.W. Turner, a champion of the Pre-Raphaelites, and a friend of Swinburne.
Italian politican during the Italian unification period. Friend of Giuseppe Mazzini.
A naiad who rejected the viriginal ways of the Greek goddess, Artemis, and whose attempted rape of Hermaphroditus led to their being eternally united as an androgynous being.
Ancient Greek lyric poet between the 6th and 7th centuries B.C.E. Born on the island of Lesbos.

person.persName: Semiramis, Queen, consort of Shamshi-Adad V, King of Assyria, 9th cent. B.C.

note.p: She was the Sammu-ramat, wife of Shamshi-Adad V of Assyria. In Greek myth, she conquered Bactria and founder Babylon; in Armenian legend, she conquered Armenia.
English Elizabethan playwright and poet, idolized by Swinburne and other Victorians. He wrote Hamlet.
English Romantic poet. Author of Prometheus Unbound. Republican.

One of the Knights of the Round Table. In the story of Tristan and Iseult, he is sent to bring Iseult from Ireland to wed his uncle, King Mark of Cornwall. Yet while returning to England, Tristan and Iseult accidentely consume a love potion and fall in love with one another.

An Italian Mannerist painter, who spent the majority of his life in Siena in the Tuscan region of central Italy. He is best known for his frescoes of St. Catherine of Siena in ecstacy after receiving the Eucharist in the San Domenico church. His last name, Bazzi, was often misrepresented as Razzi.
Athenian tragic playwright. Wrote Oedipus Rex.

In Greek mythology, a hybrid creature, part human, part animal. In Thebean legend, the sphinx was a threatening monster that lived in the western mountains of Thebes killing anyone who passed through its territory and couldn't answer its riddle.
Swinburne's youngest sister.
English dramatist.
English poet, who later became poet laureate of England. Wrote In Memoriam A.H.H..
Legendary king of Athens. In greek mythology, he slayed the Minotaur.
Most often referred to as a sea nymph in Greek mythology, but also sometimes referred to as a goddess or the creator of the universe.
In ancient Greece, a female devotee of Bacchus.
A legendary seer for the Cadmeans of Thebes, who had been given foresight to replace his loss of vision.
Friend of poets Byron and Shelley.
Roman goddess of love, beauty, and fertility. Associated with the Greek goddess, Aphrodite.
Roman goddess of the hearth and home.
Mother of famous Roman general, Coriolanus, who was exiled from Rome. Persuaded Coriolanus to not invade Rome.
French philosopher and writer. Major figure of the Enlightenment. Author of Candide.
English critic and poet. Friend of Swinburne's. Watts was instrumental in saving Swinburne from alcoholism. Swinburne lived with Watts in Putney from 1879 until Swinburne's death.
English Jacobean playwright and late contemporary of William Shakespeare. He wrote The Duchess of Malfi.
English writer best known for his nonfiction work, Sappho: memoir, text, selected renderings, and a literal translation.
American-born, English painter. Influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites. Painted Whistler's Mother.
An American poet and proponent of transcendentalism, the idea that the human mind can transcend the physical world on its own. Sometimes called the father of free verse.
English poet and Republican. Co-wrote Lyrical Ballads. One of the founders of the Romantic movement.

In ancient Greece, a female follower of Bacchus, traditionally associated with divine possession and frenzied rites. These were typically upper-class women, who, every other winter, go up into the Greek mountains to perform a ritual urged by Dionysus.

person.note: Early Welsh poet who mentions Arthur in his work.

note.p: French novelist and playwright.
English novelist. Author of Vanity Fair and The Luck of Barry Lyndon.
English philosopher and statesman; served as Attorney General and Lord Chancellor of England.
English polymath best known for his discoveries concerning the laws of gravity.
British novelist and dramatist, best known for his novel The Cloister and the Hearth.
A character in L'Homme Qui Rit, a Duchess in the English royal court who attempts to seduce Gwynplaine.
A character in L'Homme Qui Rit, a royal court agent who conspires against Duchess Josiana and orchestrates much of Gwynplaine's misfortune.
A renowned Italian Renaissance painter.

A character in Pierre Choderlos de Laclos's novel Les Liaisons dangereuses. She and her former lover, the Vicomte Sébastien de Valmont, conspire first against other members of the French nobility, then against each other.

The Roman parallel to Artemis, the Greek goddess of child birth, virginity, and the hunt. Correspondingly to Artemis, she was thought to be the twin sister to Apollo and the daughter of Jupiter and Latona.
A French poet and essayist most famous for his book of lyric poetry, Les Fleurs du mal.
In Shakespeare's play Coriolanus, she is the wife of the titular character. She pleads with her husband to make peace with Rome.
The princess of Britain and faithful wife of Posthumus in Shakespeare's Cymbeline.
The titular character of Shakespeare's King Lear, his plan to divide the kingdom of Britain amongst his three daughters ends in disaster, and he is famously driven to madness.

person.persName: Ugolino della Gherardesca, Count of Donoratico

note.p: A traitorous Italian nobleman made famous by his depiction in Dante's Inferno.
A character in Victor Hugo's L'Homme Qui Rit, she grows up with Gwynplaine after he rescues her as an infant and ultimately falls in love with him before dying tragically.
A Romani street dancer in Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris.
An English playwright whose fame was said to rival Shakespeare's.
One of the leading English poets of the 17th century.

person.persName: Armand Jean du Plessis, 1st Duke of Richelieu

note.p: A French Catholic statesman who wielded considerable power during the reign of King Louis XIII.
A French playwright, actor, and poet.
One of the prophets in the Hebrew Bible.
An Italian general who was instrumental in the creation of the Kingdom of Italy.
A Jewish prisoner. When given the choice between crucifying Jesus of Nazareth or Barabbas, the crowd of onlookers chose to crucify Jesus and release Barabbas.
A Roman poet and author of the Satires.
A Roman poet and author of De rerum natura.
In Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, the young prince of Sicily who dies tragically of a wasting disease.
A classical Greek tragedian. Notable works include Medea and The Trojan Women.
The daughter of Agamemnon, King of Mycenae, in Greek mythology. When Artemis prevents Agamemnon from coming to aid his allies in the Trojan War, he offers up Iphigenia as a human sacrifice.
In Aeschylus's Oresteia, the Queen of Mycenae who murders her husband, Agamemnon, and is in turn murdered by her son, Orestes. She is Iphigenia's mother.
A French knight and military leader, known as le chevalier sans peur et sans reproche, or the knight without fear and beyond reproach.
A politician and orator who initally played a major role in the French Revolution but spoke out against the Reign of Terror and was ultimately executed under charges of being a royalist.
An English politician and republican whose revolutionary work Discourses Concerning Government led to his being executed for treason and subsequently considered a hero and martyr.

person.persName: Nelson, Horatio, 1st Viscount Nelson, 1st Duke of Bronte

note.p: A highly renowned British naval commander who won decisive battles in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.
Served as President of France from 1871-1873. Ordered the suppression of the Paris Commune in 1871.

person.persName: Gaston Alexandre Auguste, Marquis de Galliffet, Prince de Martigues

note.p: A French general who participated in the suppression of the Paris Commune in 1871, for which he was heavily criticized.
In Christian theology, another name for Satan, or the devil.
A French journalist and author who wrote extensively in support of ultramontism, a philosophy emphasizing papal supremacy in the Catholic Church.
The first Grand Inquisitor of the Spanish Inquisition.
In Greek mythology, the son of Eos and Tithonus. An Ethiopian king who defended Troy and was killed by Achilles in the Trojan War.
A German polymath and writer.
A German poet and soldier known chiefly for his patriotic works.
A Greek poet whose works were used to inspire Spartan patriotism.
A Roman poet remembered for his bad verse.
An English poet and playwright who made a profit by presenting recycled verse in ostentatious bindings (now known as Settle bindings) to wealthy literary patrons.
A French poet and writer and an admirer of Victor Hugo. One of the founders of the Rappel.
In Greek mythology, a great warrior and the principal character in the Iliad. Fought alongside the Achaeans in the siege of Troy.
The main character of Homer's Odyssey, described as a man of twists and turns, who must use his wits to brave various trials on his way home from the Trojan War.
A British military hero and politician who played a decisive role in the Napoleonic Wars and served twice as the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
A French clergyman and diplomat.
In Petronius's Satyricon, a nouveau-riche former slave.
In Greco-Roman mythology, a Trojan hero and the ancestor of the Romans. The titular character of Virgil's Aeneid, which tells the story of Rome's founding myth.
In Greek mythology, the Argonauts were a band of heroes who accompanied Jason on his quest to find the Golden Fleece.
The antagonist in Shakespeare's Othello, considered one of Shakespeare's most sinister villains.
Othello's faithful wife in Shakespeare's eponymous play. Iago conspires to turn Othello against her.
A character in Shakespeare's Cymbeline. He attempts to seduce Imogen and turn her husband, Posthumus, against her.

A character in Shakespeare's King Lear. The youngest daughter of the titular character, she resists her father's offer of a third of his kingdom in exchange for an obsequious declaration of her love for him.
In Shakespeare's King Lear, Cordelia's power-hungry sister.

person.persName: Arthur I, 4th Earl of Richmond and Duke of Brittany

note.p: The grandson of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. At the center of a succession crisis depicted in Shakespeare's historical play, King John.

King of England from 1199 until his death. Generally believed to have killed his nephew, Arthur I, Duke of Brittany, in order to maintain a clear line of succession to the throne. The titular character of Shakespeare's King John.

One of Julius Caesar's generals. In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, he delivers the famous speech beginning, Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears, that turns the people against Caesar's assassins.
In Shakespeare's Coriolanus, the mother of the titular character who convinces him not to besiege Rome.
An Italian sculptor and architect and one of the central artistic figures of the Renaissance.
A German-British Baroque composer. Best-known works include Water Music and his oratorio Messiah.
A French Romantic writer, archaeologist, and historian. Author of the novella Carmen.
An Italian sculptor, painter, and architect.
A French novelist, poet, and dramatist.
A Greek artist, none of whose works survive. Legend has it he died of laughter.
An Italian Renaissance polymath and artist.
An Italian painter of the High Renaissance whose works and identity are somewhat of a mystery.
An Italian painter who studied under Gentile Bellini.
A French poet of the Late Middle Ages with a rather colorful criminal record. Author of Le Testament.
An Assyrian deity, depicted in a pair of statues that flanked the throne room of Ashurnasirpal II, thought to serve as protectors. Acquired by the British Museum in 1851.
English poet. Author of Sonnets from the Portuguese and Aurora Leigh.
An English theologian, originally an Anglican priest who became a Catholic cardinal. Canonized in 2019 by Pope Francis.
An Italian Renaissance painter of the Venetian School. Nicknamed il Furioso for the speed and boldness with which he painted.
An Italian Renaissance painter of the Venetian school. Best known for his large-scale paintings of elaborate narrative cycles.
English Victorian poet and novelist. Author of The Egoist.
A saint in the Catholic tradition. Sometimes called the Hammer of the Arians for his dedication to opposing Arianism in the West.
In Greek mythology, a human woman who opened a jar in which were contained all of humanity's evils. Rossetti produced a painting and multiple drawings of his muse, Jane Morris, styled as Pandora.
In Greek mythology, a prophetess of Apollo whose curse was that her prophecies, though true, would never be believed. Rossetti made a drawing of Cassandra in 1861.
In Shakespeare's Hamlet, she is driven to madness as a result of Hamlet's actions, ultimately drowning. Rossetti featured her in an oil painting and multiple drawings.
French romantic writer.

An Italian noblewoman who had an affair with her husband's brother. Famously depicted alongside her lover, Paolo Malatesta, in the circle of hell reserved for the lustful in Dante Alighieri's Inferno. Rossetti made a watercolor inspired by that scene.
In Shakespeare's Othello, a wealthy Venetian. Iago uses Roderigo's love for Othello's wife, Desdemona, to manipulate him.
In some variants of Jewish mythology, a female demonic figure held to be the first wife of Adam. The subject of an oil painting by Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
The aspect of Venus thought to turn women to sexual virtue. The subject of an oil painting by Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
A leading Roman poet during the reign of Augustus.
A Latin poet associated with the court of Honorius.
An Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance.
A prominent English writer. Author of A Dictionary of the English Language and Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets.
An English poet and politician.

An Italian noblewoman whose father abused and raped her. She and other family members conspired to kill him and were subsequently arrested and beheaded for murder despite public protests. Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote a play, The Cenci, about these events.
A character in Victor Hugo's Les Misérables. Forced into prostitution to provide for her daughter, Cosette, as a single mother, her character symbolizes loss of innocence and self-sacrifice.
An unrequited lover in Victor Hugo's poem of the same name.
An Italian Renaissance painter from Florence.

person.persName: di Mariano di Vanni Filipepi, Alessandro

note.p: An Italian painter of the Early Renaissance.
An Italian Renaissance painter among whose pupils were Sandro Botticelli, Francesco Pesellino, and Lippi's son, Filippino Lippi.
An Italian Renaissance painter. Son of Fillipo Lippi. Assisted his father and, later, Sandro Botticelli.
In Greek mythology, three thousand nymphs who were daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.
In Greek mythology, Circe was an enchantress who lived on the island of Aeaea, perhaps best known for turning Odysseus's crew into pigs in Homer's Odyssey.

In Greek mythology, a sorceress who aids Jason in his quest for the Golden Fleece. Some variations on the story include their subsequent marriage, Jason's taking another wife, and Medea's killing their children and the new bride out of revenge.
In Greek mythology, Hercules's young servant who is abducted by naiads, a type of water nymph.
In Greek mythology, the king of Iolcus who sends Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece. Medea, in a bid to obtain the throne for Jason, tricks Pelias's daughters into killing him.
A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher. Legends surrounding his death vary but tend to involve his jumping into Mount Etna, a volcano in Sicily.
In Plato's Gorgias, a philosopher who presents counter-arguments to Plato's ideas. It is unclear whether he was a real contemporary of Plato or merely a character created by Plato.
A warrior in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, he is slain by his father Rostam who does not recognize him until he has been fatally wounded.
A great hero in Persian mythology. Depicted in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.
An English poet and inspector of schools.
A French scholar whose areas of interest included Semitic languages and biblical history. Author of the Life of Jesus. Also noteworthy and controversial for his racist and white supremacist views.
A British theologian and mathematician, scholar of the Zulu language, and the first Bishop of Natal. Controversial due to his views on biblical fallibility and soteriology.

In the Hebrew Bible, traditionally understood to be a Canaanite god associated with the practice of child sacrifice. Scholars have debated whether "Moloch" refers to a deity, or to the practice of sacrifice itself.
The Hindu god of creation. With Vishnu and Shiva, part of the Trimurti, the divine trinity.

person.persName: Ghiyāth al-Dīn Abū al-Fath ʿUmar ibn Ibrāhīm Nīshābūrī

note.p: A Persian poet and polymath.
In the Hebrew Bible, a righteous man who, tested by a "satan," or adversary, suffers terrible misfortune but maintains his innocence before God.
In Greek mythology, a satyr and musician known primarily for his hubris. He is killed after challenging Apollo to, and subsequently losing, a music contest.
The wisest of the centaurs in Greek mythology. He was raised by Apollo and Artemis, trained the hero Achilles, and was known for his skill in the healing arts.

In Greek mythology, a serpentine giant who was the son of Gaia and Cronus and, along with his mate, Echidna, the father of many monsters. He attempted to overthrow Zeus, but Zeus defeated him and trapped him beneath Mount Etna.
In Greek mythology, the god of the wild, shepherds and flocks, and rustic music. Legend has it that he was the origin of the pan flute.
In Greek mythology, female members of Dionysus's revenue who were depicted as frenzied or mad women.
A Greek traveler and geographer who sought to memorialize in writing "all things Greek" in his Description of Greece.

One of the judges, or leaders, of Israel in the Hebrew Bible whose Nazirite vows granted him superhuman strength to fight against the Philistines. The subject of John Milton's dramatic poem Samson Agonistes.
In the Hebrew Bible, a king of ancient Israel who is described as being a man after God's own heart. Originally a shepherd, he defeated the Philistine giant Goliath using a sling.

In the Hebrew Bible, a Philistine of immense stature who challenged the Israelites to produce a champion who could defeat him in single combat. He was defeated by David, a shepherd, using only a sling.
The father of King David in the Hebrew Bible.

One of the judges, or leaders, of Israel in the Hebrew Bible. He led Israel to victory against the Ammonites. Perhaps best known for making a rash vow that resulted in his sacrificing his own daughter upon returning from battle.
A renowned teacher, religious and legal authority, and member of the Sanhedrin, a Jewish legislative and judicial assembly in the first century AD. He taught Paul the Apostle.
A Scottish poet.
A poet and scholar whose rediscovery of Cicero's letters is credited with starting the Italian Renaissance and founding Renaissance humanism.
The subject of Petrarch's unrequited love and many of his sonnets.

In Greek mythology, a Queen of Messenia and the wife of Cresphontes. Her husband and two elder children were murdered, and she was forced to marry the murderer; however, she was able to save her youngest son, who conspired with her to take revenge several years later. The subject of Euripides's lost tragedy, Cresphontes, which inspired Matthew Arnold's 1858 work Merope.

In Greek mythology, he murdered Cresphontes, King of Messenia, and his two eldest children and then married Cresphontes's widow, Merope. Merope and her youngest son, Aepytus, later took revenge on him.
A French moralist and essayist best known for his posthumously published Pensées. Addressed in a section of Matthew Arnold's Essays in Criticism.
In Greek mythology, the wife of Hercules. She is tricked into soaking his tunic in poison, resulting in his death, after which she takes her own life.
The son of Zeus and Callisto in Greek mythology. He was a famous hunter and king of Arcadia.

In Greek mythology, a follower of Artemis who was impregnated by Zeus and bore a son, Arcas. Hera, furious, turned her into a bear. Zeus set her in the sky as the constellation Ursa Major to prevent her from being killed by her unwitting son.

The headmaster and later provost of Eton College. He had a reputation for his facility with language and as a writer of English hexameters. Matthew Arnold referred to his translation of a passage from the Iliad as the most successful attempt hitherto made at rendering Homer into English.
An English poet and the subject of Matthew Arnold's elegy Thyrsis.
An English professor, social reformer, historian, novelist, poet, and priest of the Church of England.
In Roman mythology, the god of beginnings, endings, transitions, doorways, and duality. Typically depicted with a double-sided head.

A god worshipped in ancient Syria and, in the Hebrew Bible, by the Philistines. According to the Hebrew Bible, when the Philistines captured the Ark of the Covenant and brought it to the house of Dagon in Ashdod, the statue of Dagon fell on its face repeatedly before the ark. Samson's final act in the book of Judges is to destroy the temple of Dagon in Gaza.
The Duke of Orléans and a prolific medieval poet in both French and English.
A French poet, dramatist, novelist, journalist, and critic.
A French poet remarkable for his intense passion for nature.
Alongside Molière and Corneille, one of the three great playwrights of 17th-century France.
An English Enlightenment poet, translator, and satirist.
A French poet and critic. Friend of Molière and Jean Racine.
A French literary critic. He had connections to Victor Hugo's literary circle but was estranged after having an affair with Hugo's wife.
A French Catholic priest, philosopher, and political theorist who championed the separation of church and state.

In Greek mythology, the mother of Dionysus by Zeus. Hera tricks her into asking Zeus to show her his full glory; as a mortal, she cannot withstand the sight and is incinerated. Zeus saves her fetal son, Dionysus, by sewing him into his own thigh. Dionysus later rescues Semele from Hades, and she becomes a goddess on Mount Olympus.
An English poet and hymnwriter who was one of the forerunners of Romantic poetry.
A French writer. Sister of Maurice de Guérin.

person.persName: Teresa Sánchez de Cepeda Dávila y Ahumada

death.date: At some hour of the night between 4 October and 15 October 1582, the night of the transition in Spain from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar.

note.p: A prominent Spanish mystic and nun whose desire for religious reform led her to establish the Order of Discalced Carmelites. Author of The Interior Castle.
An Italian mystic and laywoman who tended to the sick in Siena, wrote extensively about theology, and had considerable influence with the papacy.
An Italian noblewoman and poet.

In the Hebrew Bible, Samson falls in love with Delilah. Bribed by the lords of the Philistines, she convinces Samson to reveal the secret of his strength, namely, his uncut hair. She cuts his hair while he sleeps and turns him over to the Philistines.
The editor of the Revue des deux Mondes from 1831 to 1877. Brought in works from such renowned French authors as Victor Hugo, Alexandre Dumas, and Honoré de Balzac.
A French art and literary critic who contributed to the Revue des deux Mondes.

person.persName: Armand Augustin Joseph Marie Ferrard, Comte de Pontmartin

note.p: A French journalist, critic, and man of letters. Best known for his satirical novel, Les Jeudis de Madame Charbonneau, in which he humorously depicts his contemporaries.

A French literary critic who contributed several pieces to the Revue des deux Mondes. In Le Paganisme poétique en Angleterre: John Keats et Algernon Charles Swinburne, he compares Keats and Swinburne and criticizes both of them.

A god of Germanic and Norse mythology. When Baldr prophetically dreamt of his own death, his mother made every object on the earth promise not to harm him. The mistletoe alone did not make this promise, and Loki used a spear or arrow made of mistletoe to kill him.
